extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, taxonomy, and scientific classification (naturalists, philosophers of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on forming, arranging, and using scientific/taxonomic classifications and diagnostic (dichotomous) keys, including the logical foundations (predicables, abstraction, Logical Alphabet) and practical criteria for selecting diagnostic characters. Useful for constructing classification schemes and identification keys in natural science and logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus (one of the Five Predicables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus: any class of objects regarded as broken up into two minor classes (species). Interpreted with respect to intension (a group of qualities) and extension (a group of objects possessing those qualities). The genus is defined by a certain number of qualities or circumstances which belong to all objects included in the class, and which are sufficient to mark out these objects from all others which we do not intend to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genus denotes the common qualities sufficient to delimit a class; when designing a classification pick the genus-level qualities that are shared by all intended members. (Text examples and discussion of intension vs extension illustrate how a genus contains species by adding differences.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Species (one of the Five Predicables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Species: a minor class formed by dividing a genus by a difference. Interpreted in intension (contains the genus plus one more quality—the difference) and in extension (is a portion of the genus' objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A species should be defined by the genus plus a specific difference; treat species either as more intensionally specified or as smaller extensions of the genus. Use species definitions to separate members practically and logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference (one of the Five Predicables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference: a quality which, being possessed by some of the objects and not by others, divides the genus into two species. The difference can be interpreted in intension only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose differences that clearly partition a genus into distinct species; differences are the successive critical differentiae used in bifurcate (dichotomous) keys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property (one of the Five Predicables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Property: a quality which belongs to the whole of a class but does not enter into the definition of that class. A generic property belongs to every individual object in the genus; a specific property follows from the difference and belongs to the species. A 'peculiar property' belongs only to that class and allows a statement as a simple identity (A = B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize properties as consequences correlated with the defining qualities rather than as defining marks. Peculiar properties are valuable because they enable simple identity statements (example: a curve of equal curvature = curve of greatest area for the circle). Use properties to infer further attributes of class members but do not necessarily use them as defining characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident (one of the Five Predicables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accident: any quality which may or may not belong to certain objects and has no connection with the adopted classification (i.e., not correlated with the species' definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use accidental qualities as defining characters; they are irrelevant to the logical classification and will not help diagnosis (examples: absolute size of a plant, manner of crystal grouping in crystallographic classification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Alphabet / combinatorial completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Logical Alphabet represents combinations of qualities and thus an interminable series of subordinate genera and species; in strict logic one must contemplate all sanctioned combinations of notions by the laws of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming classifications, be conscious that logical possibilities (combinatorial combinations of qualities) extend beyond observed instances. The Logical Alphabet is the conceptual limit of class combinations; use it to reason about potential species and to ensure classificatory completeness in a logical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summum genus / infima species must be relative
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no absolute summum genus (a genus generalissimum) because every class implies a negative/contrast; likewise the infima species may be individual objects. Relative to a branch of knowledge there will be terminal genera or species bounding the horizon of that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design classifications with awareness that the topmost and bottommost ranks are relative to the subject matter and purpose. Restricting a classification to a field (chemist, mathematician, naturalist) is acceptable and often necessary; do not assume an absolute universal top or bottom of the hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction implies generalisation (logical rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever we abstract a quality or circumstance we generalise or widen the notion; e.g., AB is mentally wider than ABC because AB includes both ABC and ABc. Abstraction increases extent while decreasing intension according to inverse relation of logical quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constructing classes, recognize that omitting differences produces more general terms that (logically) include more possible species. Be cautious about equating abstraction with merely listing existing instances — abstraction opens classification to possible or future combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include places for possible/imaginary combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A purely logical classification must take account not only of what certainly exists but of what may in after ages be found to exist, and we must have places in our scientific classifications for purely imaginary existences (mathematical functions, speculative physical worlds) unless forbidden by fundamental laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confine a classification solely to currently known objects: for logical completeness allow slots for conceivable combinations; this helps in theoretical work and mathematical/physical reasoning. However, balance this with practical purposes when building working identification systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize logical impossibility / mathematical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Some combinations of qualities are entirely forbidden by mathematical or other certain laws (e.g., a circle not having the maximal-area-for-perimeter property or a parallelogram lacking equal opposite angles would be non-existent species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When enumerating logical combinations, exclude those combinations demonstrably impossible by laws of geometry, arithmetic, physics, etc. Use domain knowledge to eliminate impossible species from classificatory schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic (diagnostic) marks — logical conditions of a good characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic is any conspicuous and easily discriminated property selected to decide the class of an object. The logical conditions of a good characteristic are: it should be possessed by all objects entering into a certain class and by none others; every characteristic should enable a simple identity (A = B). The characteristic may be a single quality or a group, provided they are constant and easily detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select characteristics that are constant across the class and absent elsewhere, so they yield reliable identities. Prefer marks that are conspicuous and can be observed readily (examples: leaf venation, flower part counts, particular teeth in mammals). Avoid characteristics that are frequently absent or hard to observe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observable correlates when deep defining qualities are impractical to detect
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the deepest or most important points (defining qualities) are not the ones most readily observed; choose correlated conspicuous characters to enable diagnosis (e.g., seed-leaf number correlates with leaf venation and flower part counts in plants; starch production correlates with vegetable vs animal distinction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical diagnostic systems, use easily observed correlates of the defining criteria so identification is feasible in the field or routine practice. Be aware of exceptions (cotyledons obsolete or united) and avoid relying on a single correlate when it can mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic procedure and limits of definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnosis consists in comparing the qualities of an object with class definitions: absence of any one quality excludes the object from that class; if every point of a definition is exactly fulfilled, assign the object to that class. But definitions can only enumerate a finite number of qualities and cannot guarantee truth for all future objects; individuals cannot be defined (only exhibited or represented by specimens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply diagnosis by sequentially testing definition points; accept that assignment is probabilistic rather than infallible. Maintain specimen records and material exemplars for individuals because definitions cannot fully capture unique instances. Use diagnostic keys to operationalize comparisons but keep in mind the epistemic limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic (bifurcate/dichotomous) systems — recommended arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnostic systems of classification should, as a general rule, be arranged on the bifurcate method explicitly: choose any quality that divides the group into two parts and subdivide each part by successive prominent and well-marked circumstances present in a large part of one side and not the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating identification keys, use dichotomous successive discriminations (yes/no splits) for ease of referral: note whether the specimen does or does not possess successive critical differentiae. Examples: Dana's crystal key, Von Kobell's blow-pipe mineral divisions, Bentham's analytical key for British flora. Be mindful that extensive bifurcate tables can become unwieldy and labour-intensive to construct; weigh logical value against practical economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose discriminating qualities that are prominent, well-marked, and present in many members
rubrics_metrics.description: Any quality chosen for division should be prominent and well-marked, present in a large part of the genus and absent in the other, so that successive divisions are effective for referral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer discriminators that yield large, stable groupings early in a key to minimize wicker-work of tiny branches; numerical discriminations are acceptable but can make dichotomous exhibitions tedious. Arrange the order of discriminations to maximize ease and reliability of identification (use counts of petals, stamens, etc., only when reliable and not too laborious).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical conservatism: prefer the most constant characters and avoid negative reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxonomists prefer to trust to those characteristic characters which are most constant; avoid employing a characteristic negatively (i.e., excluding by absence) when it may mislead (example: Diatomaceae probably vegetables though they do not produce starch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In building keys and diagnoses, prefer positive, constant, and observable characters; be cautious using absence-of-feature as a decisive exclusion unless absence is a very reliable discriminator.
